extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature, philosophy, and comedy; comic artists and playwrights
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical/literary analysis of what makes forms, gestures, movements and social phenomena laughable; identifies mechanisms (automatism, caricature, disguise, repetition, etc.) that produce comic effects and gives examples and counterexamples. Useful for theorizing or creating comic material in performance, drawing, or writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitable deformity as comic criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A deformity that may become comic is a deformity that a normally built person could successfully imitate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a physical peculiarity can be mimicked by an otherwise 'normal' body, it becomes laughable because imitation reveals its mechanical or stereotyped nature. Example: the hunchback suggests a posture anyone could adopt; that potential for imitation underlies its comic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic expression = fixed permanent grimace
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic expression of the face is one that promises nothing more than it gives. It is a unique and permanent grimace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with expressive beauty where a stable expression is nevertheless imagined as mobile. A comic face appears stereotyped, crystallized, as if the whole moral life were absorbed into one mechanical cast of features (always weeping, always laughing, always whistling). This permanence/uniqueness is central to its comic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatism / inelasticity / habitual rigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatism, inelasticity, habit that has been contracted and maintained are the causes why a face (or gesture) makes us laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic increases when these visible habits can be connected to a deeper absentmindedness (soul fascinated by materiality). Habitual, machine-like behavior signals loss of living variability and yields laughter. Examples: ingrained twitching, fixed grimace, repetitive gestures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature as magnification of embryonic tendency
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of the caricaturist consists in detecting an imperceptible tendency and rendering it visible by magnifying it; exaggeration must reveal an existing inclination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration is comic only if it appears as a means to make nascent distortions visible, not as an end in itself. Good caricature respects the ground-plan of a feature and lengthens or alters it in the direction nature already tends, creating the sense that the original determined to 'grin' or distort itself. Poor caricature merely grotesquely exaggerates without revealing an underlying tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form as outline of movement (exaggerate implied vectors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form is always the outline of a movement; even immobile elements (nose curve, ear shape) should be exaggerated in the direction of the movement they imply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful comic alteration lengthens or shifts a feature along the vector it was already 'going' in, so the feature looks like it has decided to perform the grimace prescribed by its shape. This preserves believability while producing comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic contrasts with gracefulness (rigidity vs suppleness)
rubrics_metrics.description: To define the comic by comparison, it should be contrasted with gracefulness rather than with beauty; the comic partakes of rigidness rather than ugliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effects often arise from the failure of the body's suppleness: when matter resists the soul's animation and petrifies its movements, the result is comic. Thus emphasis should be on loss of grace/mobility rather than conventional ugliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-like suggestion in gestures/movements
rubrics_metrics.description: The attitudes, gestures and movements of the human body are laughable in exact proportion as that body reminds us of a mere machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic drawings, performances, or descriptions should make the viewer perceive simultaneously a living person and, through or behind them, a mechanical set-up. The suggestion must be both clear (we see the machine image) and subtle (the person still seems alive). Examples: stiff, puppet-like movement; actors moving as if joined by invisible threads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and subtlety of the machine-person image
rubrics_metrics.description: The suggestion must be a clear one (we must distinctly perceive a set-up mechanism) and also a subtle one (the person must still give the impression of a living being).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more exactly the images of person and machine fit, the stronger the comic effect and the greater the draughtsman's or actor's art. Over-explicitness or bluntness that destroys the living aspect weakens subtle comic effect; overly obscure suggestion fails to register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and identicalness produce laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement always the same, repeating at regular intervals, makes us laugh because we then have before us a machine that works automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition signals automatism; if a gesture becomes predictable and expected, laughter follows. This applies in speech and stage gesture (a public speaker whose repeated head or arm movement is awaited) and in the pairing of two identical faces. Repetition that mimics life rather than follows living variability provokes laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation reveals automatism and is laughable
rubrics_metrics.description: Gestures that were not laughable become laughable when imitated by another individual, because imitation exposes their mechanical uniformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To imitate someone is to highlight the element of automatism in them; imitation therefore is a reliable device for producing laughter. Parody commonly uses imitation, sometimes deflecting gestures toward mechanical occupations to make them more evidently machine-like (e.g., sawing wood, striking an anvil).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity/uniformity (marionette effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several characters performing the same attitudes and motions (absolute uniformity) make us think of marionettes; the invisible threads and absolute uniformity intensify the comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choreography or stage business that synchronizes many bodies in identical movement evokes puppetry and mechanization, increasing laughter. The more the group resembles automata, the stronger the comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic devices as clockwork arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: The usual devices of comedy (periodical repetition of a word/scene, systematic inversion of parts, geometrical development of farce, etc.) derive their comic force from setting before us an obvious clockwork arrangement of human events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights should aim to reveal mechanical schematics behind believable surface probability; comedic structure that foregrounds the ‘mechanism’ behind actions creates humor. The art consists in balancing an outward aspect of probability with a visible mechanism underneath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguise/fashion as source of comic (incongruity of covering vs covered)
rubrics_metrics.description: A garment or fashion becomes laughable when its rigidity or incongruity with the living body makes the covering appear as a disguise; a sudden dissolution of continuity (breaking fashion) revives the comic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiar clothing tends to fuse with the person and suppress comic perception; novelty or historical eccentricity that isolates garment from person invites laughter. Comic effect arises when the inert rigidity of clothes clashes with the living suppleness underneath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of artifice/disguise even where none exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination treats inherent features as if they were artificially laid on (e.g., a black face imagined as daubed with soot, a red nose as painted), passing the quality of disguise onto natural attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise or incongruity can make us interpret natural variation as disguise; this transfer amplifies comic effects. Writers/performers can exploit this by framing or suggesting artificiality in otherwise natural traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremony, formality and stereotyped social acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Any ceremony or formula, once isolated in imagination from its serious object, loses seriousness and becomes comic; form or formula is a ready-made frame into which comic element may be fitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stereotyped social actions (ceremonies, official routines) suggest automatism and can be mined for comedy by isolating their form. Examples: a solemn sitting of a court turned comic by focusing on the ceremonial gestures; officials performing duties 'like a machine' (e.g., customs officers asking shipwreck survivors if they have anything to declare).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedantry / administrative regulation supplanting natural laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The human regulation of affairs usurping the place of the laws of nature (pedantry: art pretending to outdo nature) is comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rules, regulations, or erudite argumentation override common-sense experience, the mismatch produces comedy. Examples: a philosopher saying 'Experience is in the wrong'; doctors whose learned reasoning produces absurd clinical outcomes (Molière's doctors). This is a higher-level transfer of the mechanical-on-living idea into social/ideational spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body interrupting the moral / physical intruding on the intellectual
rubrics_metrics.description: Any incident is comic that calls our attention to the physical in a person, when it is the moral side that is concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moments when bodily needs or accidents intrude into serious, moral, or intellectual contexts produce laughter (e.g., sneezing at the pathetic moment of a speech; a funeral sentence 'He was virtuous and plump'). Comedy arises from the sudden shift of attention from soul/moral to body/physical.
